title: The Siege Begins and a Prophet's Loss
overview: On the day Babylon's army surrounds Jerusalem, Ezekiel uses a cooking pot and then the sudden death of his own wife as signs that the city and its temple are about to fall.

parts.label: Write down this date (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Ezekiel, living far away among the exiles in Babylon, is told to record the exact day the siege of Jerusalem starts. The date matches the one given in 2 Kings, so when news later arrived, it would show his message was reliable.

parts.label: The cooking pot (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Jerusalem's leaders had boasted that their city was like a pot and they were the meat, meaning they were safe inside its walls. Here the image is turned around: the city is a pot on the fire, and the people, even the finest of them, will be cooked in it.

parts.label: Blood left on bare rock (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: The law of Moses said spilled blood should be covered with earth, but Jerusalem's killings were done so openly that no one even tried to hide them. So God leaves that blood exposed, as if crying out for justice, and the meat is pulled out piece by piece, a picture of the people being taken one after another.

parts.label: A pot that will not come clean (vv. 9-14)
parts.note: After the meat is gone, the empty pot is set on the coals to burn off a crust that nothing else could remove, a picture of the city itself being burned. The point is that warnings had failed, and now judgment will come without holding back.

parts.label: Ezekiel's wife dies (vv. 15-18)
parts.note: God tells Ezekiel that the 'delight of his eyes' will be taken suddenly, and that evening his wife dies. He may groan quietly but must skip the usual mourning customs: baring his head and feet, covering his lower face, and eating the meal neighbors brought to grieving families.

parts.label: What his silence means (vv. 19-27)
parts.note: Like his wife, the temple, the people's pride and joy, will be destroyed, and the children left behind in Jerusalem will die. The people will not mourn in the usual ways either, though scholars differ on exactly why, and when a survivor brings the news, Ezekiel's long silence will end.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether to read verse 16 as God directly causing Ezekiel's wife to die for the sake of a sign, or as God foretelling a death and giving it meaning, and that choice shapes how the whole second half is understood.
think: When a loss is too big for the usual ways of grieving, what do people do with it?
